Compare temples

Pick two temples to see them side by side — height, date, dynasty, deity and what makes each one special.

Parasuramesvara Temple

Mukteshvara Temple

Parasuramesvara Temple is about 2.9 m taller than Mukteshvara Temple — about 1.3× as tall.

Parasuramesvara Temple
Date
c. 7th–8th century CE Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2,3,4]
For curious grown-ups

No building inscription is known, so every date comes from style or letter shapes. Panigrahi (1961) said about 650 CE; Brown (1959) towards the end of the 8th century; R.D. Banerji (reported by Panigrahi) not before the 8th century, from the planet labels on the door. Older writers said about 500 CE (Fergusson, 1876) and the 9th century (Mitra, 1880).

Dynasty
Shailodbhava period Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,4]
For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) placed it in Shailodbhava times, based on his own date of about 650 CE, but wrote that we do not know whether any Shailodbhava ruler built temples here. Fergusson (1876) thought it 'may belong to the preceding dynasty', before his Kesari kings.

Height
about 13 m (44 ft) Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [2]
For curious grown-ups

Only one set of figures was found: Percy Brown (1959) gives 44 ft for the tower and 48 ft for the shrine and hall together. This is not an ASI measurement. Fergusson (1876) gives only the plan, about 20 ft square.

Deity
Shiva or Vishnu Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,3,4]
For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) notes carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra (1880) reports that the Ekamra Purana names its god Daityesvara. Fergusson (1876) judged it a Vishnu temple from its name and its wall carvings.

Temple type
triratha (three-strip plan) Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [5,6]
For curious grown-ups

Ganguly (1912) twice calls this temple's main shrine (vimana) a triratha dewl, which he defines as 'having one central pilaster or Rahapaga, and two Konaka pagas, or end pilasters'. Debala Mitra's ASI glossary gives the same meaning: a central projection (raha) divides each wall into three, the two outer ones (kanika) on the same plane. No source checked calls any part of this temple pancharatha (five-strip).

What's special

Look at the doorway of the holy room. A carved stone slab shows the planet gods, each with its name cut into the stone beside it. But one is missing! Ketu, the ninth planet god, is left out. Later temples, such as Mukteshvara, added him. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) notes that Ketu is absent from the planet slabs of all the early temples up to the end of the 9th century.

Now look up at the tower. It is short and sturdy, with heavy shoulders. On top sits a very wide crowning stone with ribs around it. The tower's shape is simple, like a first draft. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959) called the tower 'thick-set and heavy-shouldered', with an 'immensely wide' ribbed crowning stone, and its shape 'rudimentary'.

The tower is covered with carvings. You can spot arch-shaped window designs, ribbed stone discs, shallow niches and round medallions. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961): 'The Chaitya arches, bhumi-amalakas, shallow niches and medallions that decorate the sikhara of the Parasuramesvara are to be found in the similar positions of the Sisiresvara also.' (The scan's text is damaged at 'bhumi-amalakas'.)

Mukteshvara Temple
Date
c. 966–975 CE Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2]
For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959) judged from details of its style that it was 'probably built about' 975 CE. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) argued for 966 CE. He took that year from a palm-leaf manuscript verse about a Shiva temple, and linked it to this temple through a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Panigrahi also places it between the Sisiresvara (c. 800 CE) and the Brahmesvara (c. 1060 CE). No inscription dates the temple.

Dynasty
Somavamshi (Kesari) Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1]
For curious grown-ups

This is one scholar's view. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) bases it on the temple's style and on a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it, whom he identifies as the Somavamshi ruler Yayati I. Percy Brown (1959) dates the temple but names no dynasty in the passage checked. No inscription links the temple to a dynasty.

Height
about 10.5 m (35 ft) Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]
For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959): the tower is 'hardly 35 feet high'. K.C. Panigrahi (1961): 'a height of only 34' feet, with an unclear fraction in the scan text. Rajendralala Mitra (1880) gives 'barely 3S feet' (scan text unclear: 35 or 38). None of these is an ASI measurement.

Deity
Not yet verified — see our content policy.
Temple type
pancharatha shrine with pidha jagamohana Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]
For curious grown-ups

This description follows K.C. Panigrahi's 1961 study of the temple.

What's special

Stand in front of the temple and you will see a free-standing gateway called a torana (arched gateway). Two carved pillars hold up a round arch above it. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2,3]

This arch is one of the most original ideas in the whole Odisha style. No other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has one quite like it. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,2]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959) called it 'one of the most original conceptions throughout the entire style'. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) noted that no other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has such an arch.

People have long admired its beauty. Some old writers called it a gem of Odisha architecture. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2,4]

For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959) called it 'a miniature gem of architecture'. James Fergusson (1876) wrote that, in its class, it was 'the gem of Orissan architecture'.
